metadata.title: Why Neural Networks Need a Bend
metadata.audience: makers and curious learners new to ML

beats.narration_text: Jambo, this is Liam, in for Bear. The ask: why does every neural network put a bend between its layers? Wouldn't stacking more straight layers be enough? Show me with real numbers.

show.event: composer card fades in on cream
greeting 'Jambo, Liam' types above the composer
the ask types in
runningText 'multiplying it out…' appears
three result lines cascade in

props.segment: Why Neural Networks Need a Bend
props.command: Why does every neural network put a bend between its layers? Wouldn't stacking more straight layers be enough? Show me with real numbers.
output: two straight layers multiply out to one: identical outputs, executed
XOR: 115,560 lines tried, the best gets 3 of 4
one ReLU bend solves it; trained from 100 seeds, it finds it 18 times

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — ask lands answered; Liam introduced in first breath.

beats.narration_text: A bend between layers makes a network powerful. Stacking alone isn't enough: straight layers, however many, collapse into one. Add a simple bend between them, and the network can finally draw a curve.

show.event: cream page holds; caret blinks
types 'Stacking more layers / makes a network powerful.'
'Stacking more layers' turns terracotta, hesitates, backspaces
types 'A bend between layers'
final lines settle: 'A bend between layers / makes a network powerful.'

props.text:
Stacking more layers
makes a network powerful.

beats.role_note: EXECUTIVE-SUMMARY LAW — misconception corrected: depth alone is not what gives a network its power; the nonlinearity between layers is.

beats.narration_text: Two moves build a plain neural network. The first is a layer: multiply by a matrix. It can stretch, rotate and shear the plane, but straight lines stay straight, and parallel lines stay parallel. The second is the bend, here a ReLU: keep positive numbers, flatten negatives to zero. That one creases the plane. A network alternates the two: layer, bend, layer.

show.event: a square grid of the input plane draws on, axes in ink
label 'layer = multiply by a matrix' (MathTex Wx)
grid shears and rotates under a 2×2 matrix; every grid line stays straight and parallel
inset: ReLU graph, flat at zero for z<0, slope 1 for z>0 (MathTex ReLU(z)=max(0,z))
grid passes through ReLU: negative halves fold flat onto the axes; creases light terracotta
the word 'bend' in the ReLU header is boxed in ink on 'layer, bend, layer'

shot.visual_intent: The framework: a layer is a linear map (lines stay lines); the bend is ReLU (it creases).
shot.motion_claim: The same grid undergoes both moves on cue, so 'straight stays straight' vs 'creased' is seen, not told.

beats.narration_text: Here are two straight layers with no bend: seeded random matrices. Push the input, minus one, two, through the first layer: minus one, minus three. Then the second: seven, eight. Now multiply the two matrices first, into one. Push the same input through that single matrix: seven, eight. Identical. Two layers were one layer in disguise.

show.event: left path: W₁x = (−1, −3) lands under W₁
left path: W₂(W₁x) = (7, 8)
right path: W₂W₁ multiplies out to [[-5, 1], [-8, 0]] (one matrix)
right path: (W₂W₁)x = (7, 8)
MathTex W₂(W₁x) = (W₂W₁)x between the two results; terracotta BOX on the '='

shot.visual_intent: Two computation paths side by side with executed integer matrices (demo/evidence.json).
shot.motion_claim: Both paths compute in narration order and land on the same vector, held side by side ≥2 s.

beats.narration_text: Not a lucky pick. A thousand random inputs, ten random layers in a row. Multiply the ten matrices into one, and every output lands on top of the stack's output. The largest gap is in the fifteenth decimal place: rounding, not structure. Add a shift to each layer, a bias, and you still get one matrix plus one shift. Depth without a bend buys no new shapes.

show.event: a cloud of 1,000 input points (seed 1)
the cloud morphs through ten linear layers, one after another (layer counter 1→10)
a ghost cloud from the single multiplied-out matrix lands exactly on top
counter: largest difference 8.88e-15 (MathTex 8.88×10⁻¹⁵), chip 'float rounding'
MathTex W₂(W₁x + b₁) + b₂ = (W₂W₁)x + (W₂b₁ + b₂) typesets; terracotta box on the right-hand side

shot.visual_intent: Ten-layer linear stack vs its single multiplied-out matrix on 1,000 executed inputs.
shot.motion_claim: The two clouds coincide; the difference counter shows only rounding error.

beats.narration_text: Now a problem no straight map can touch. XOR: output one when exactly one input is on. Four corners of a square, the ones on one diagonal, the zeros on the other. Find a single line with both ones on one side. We tried over a hundred and fifteen thousand. The best gets three of four, and four lines of algebra prove no line ever gets all four.

show.event: unit square; corners (0,0),(1,1) as hollow ink circles '0', (0,1),(1,0) as filled ink dots '1'
a line sweeps and rotates across the square; a 'correct: n of 4' counter flickers
tally: 'lines tried 115,560' climbs; 'best: 3 of 4' locks
the best line freezes with one point on the wrong side, ringed terracotta
the four inequalities typeset (MathTex) and add to a contradiction

shot.visual_intent: XOR's four points and an exhaustive line sweep that never exceeds 3 of 4 (executed).
shot.motion_claim: The sweep is the search; the counter maxing at 3 is the result; the algebra closes it.

beats.narration_text: So give it depth. A two-layer network with no bend, trained by gradient descent for five thousand steps. The loss sinks to zero point two five and flattens. Every output settles at one half: a shrug. That's exactly what the best single line predicts, because this network is a single line. A hundred seeds, same floor. None gets all four.

show.event: network strip x → W₁ → W₂ → y with the bend slot visibly empty
loss curve plots over 5,000 steps (every 250, executed) and flattens at 0.25
four output bars settle at 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5 against targets 0, 1, 1, 0
beside them: least-squares best line predicts 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5; terracotta '=' box joins the two
chip: '100 seeds: lowest loss 0.25, all four right: 0'

shot.visual_intent: A trained deep linear net lands on the best line's answer: one half everywhere (executed).
shot.motion_claim: The loss curve flattens as narrated; the bars and the best-line bars match side by side.

beats.narration_text: Now add one bend. Two hidden units, weights set by hand, from the Deep Learning textbook. Each unit adds up the inputs; the second also subtracts one. Then the ReLU. At zero, zero, the second unit reads minus one, and the ReLU flattens it to zero. The output takes the first unit minus twice the second. Zero, one, one, zero. XOR, exactly.

show.event: MathTex h = ReLU(Wx + c), y = w·h with W, c, w as matrices; caption 'weights: Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville (2016), §6.1'
table header x | Wx + c | ReLU | y | target
row x=(0, 0): z=(0, −1) → h=(0, 0); terracotta box on the −1 → 0 clip
y column fills 0, 1, 1, 0 and matches the target column, row by row ✓

shot.visual_intent: The hand-set 2-unit ReLU network computing XOR row by row (executed, asserted).
shot.motion_claim: Each row lands on its spoken cue; the single clip is the beat's terracotta moment.

beats.narration_text: Here's what the bend did, geometrically. The first layer lays all four points on one line, and the two ones land on the same spot, stuck between the zeros. ReLU folds that line at the corner, pulling the zero, zero point up to the origin. Now one straight line separates them. Unfold it back to the square, and that line becomes a band: ones inside, zeros out.

show.event: input square with the four XOR points
linear move to (z₁, z₂): points slide onto the line z₂ = z₁ − 1; the two '1' points merge at (1, 0)
ReLU fold: the part of that line below the axis folds up; (0, −1) lands on (0, 0); the crease glows terracotta
line h₁ − 2h₂ = ½ draws, the merged '1' on one side, both '0's on the other
unfold back to the input square: the region becomes a band between x₁ + x₂ = ½ and x₁ + x₂ = 3⁄2

shot.visual_intent: The geometry of the fold: hidden space before/after ReLU and the band it carves in the input plane.
shot.motion_claim: The points physically move through the linear map and the fold; the separator appears only after the fold.

beats.narration_text: So is the bend enough? Same two-unit network, but now trained from a hundred random starts instead of set by hand. Here, eighteen find XOR. Eighty-two get stuck, most with a hidden unit that went flat and never woke up. The bend makes a solution possible; it doesn't make training find it. Give it eight units, and ninety-one of a hundred succeed.

show.event: 10×10 grid of seed tiles, labelled 'seeds 0–99, 2 hidden units'
tiles resolve in seed order: solved = ink check, stuck = hollow; counter climbs to 18 / 100
inset for stuck seed 0: one hidden unit flat at zero on all four inputs, outputs 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5; terracotta ring on the flat unit
chip: '69 of 82 stuck runs have a dead unit'
a second grid '8 hidden units' resolves beside it: 91 / 100

shot.visual_intent: 100 seeded training runs at two widths: the bend is necessary, not sufficient (executed).
shot.motion_claim: The two grids are side by side and held, so 18 vs 91 is a visible comparison, not a spoken one.

beats.narration_text: And the bend has a shape. Walk the hand-set network along the square's diagonal. The output is flat, then climbs in a straight line, then falls in a straight line. Two kinks, exactly where a unit switches on. Keep walking past the data and it never curves back: at three, three it says minus four. Between and beyond its kinks, a ReLU network is made of straight pieces.

show.event: inset square with the diagonal x = (t, t) marked; main axes t vs y
output traces left to right: flat 0, then up to 1 at t = ½, then down
terracotta dots on the two kinks at t = 0 and t = ½; labels 'unit 1 on', 'unit 2 on'
trace continues past t = 1 with no curve: (3, 3) → −4
MathTex pieces: y = 0, y = 2t, y = 2 − 2t (straight pieces bracketed)

shot.visual_intent: Piecewise-linear output of the hand-set net along the diagonal, executed (demo/evidence.json).
shot.motion_claim: The trace draws in order; the kinks are marked where the narration says 'switches on'.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. A layer multiplies by a matrix: straight lines stay straight. Stacked layers without a bend multiply out to one matrix. XOR has no separating line, so no purely linear network learns it. One ReLU bend folds the plane; two hidden units solve XOR exactly. The bend makes a solution possible, not easy to find. Between and beyond its kinks, a ReLU network is made of straight pieces.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: Write a short Python script using only numpy. Train a tiny network on XOR twice: once with no activation, once with a ReLU and two hidden units. Use plain gradient descent from twenty random seeds each, and print how many seeds get all four points right. Then, from the printed numbers alone, explain why the linear version never succeeds and why the ReLU version sometimes fails. Here's what to check. The linear runs should never get all four right, on any seed. For the ReLU runs that fail, ask Claude to print the hidden units, and look for one stuck at zero. And make sure the explanation comes from the printed numbers, not a recited theorem.
